name: Embrace
label: Dischord
lede: Embrace played nine shows in under a year, and the album came out a year after they split. It's where Ian MacKaye slowed hardcore down to see what else it could say.

eras.title: Slower, on purpose
eras.text: Two years after Minor Threat, MacKaye wanted out of the violence that had swallowed hardcore shows, not out of punk. Embrace kept the fire and dropped the tempo, then pointed the songs at greed, self-delusion and the scene itself, right as Revolution Summer was remaking D.C.

years.h: MacKaye joins three ex-members of Faith
years.p: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] teams up with [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]], [[Chris Bald|0838359b-95a7-48e9-a9f6-0e8f40bb34d2]] and [[Ivor Hanson|a17981f7-ab3d-46dc-859a-582ac894cb20]], all late of [[Faith|f735a867-9a16-451f-8f83-669ed42e2574]], the band his brother [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]] fronted. Hampton and Hanson go back further, to [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]].

years.h: First show: Food for Thought, Dupont Circle
years.p: Embrace debut in the middle of Revolution Summer at a former restaurant-turned-venue. MacKaye's new band is slower, more melodic and more inward than anything he'd fronted before.
years.xp:
AllMusic described the band as having the fire and passion of hardcore, albeit slower and more heartfelt. Dischord points to small rooms and a personal, introspective take on punk.

Across town, [[Rites of Spring|b2ff1a6d-9198-4646-b068-8965242d245b]] were pulling the same way. Between the two bands, D.C. hardcore was learning a new register.

eras.title: Nine shows, then quiet
eras.text: Embrace finished the record and simply stopped. By spring MacKaye was in London recording as Egg Hunt with his old Minor Threat drummer Jeff Nelson, Hampton had joined three ex-Rites of Spring members in One Last Wish, and the Embrace album sat on a shelf.

years.h: The ninth show, at the 9:30 Club, is the last
years.p: Embrace split after March 1986 at the 9:30 Club, nine shows in. AllMusic called the breakup unceremonious, and nobody in the band has given a reason on the record.
years.xp:
The four scattered fast. Hampton went to [[One Last Wish|94f18045-7fe2-41df-bf24-0bed21c88eb8]], Bald to [[Ignition|3cb2b7d6-1f0b-4ac5-b67f-52132f3d3b61]], and Hanson reunited with Hampton in Manifesto. MacKaye tried a few things before landing on Fugazi.

A fan recording of the 9:30 Club set circulates in full, about 28 minutes.

years.h: MacKaye and Nelson record four songs in London as [[Egg Hunt|2d8d08d8-c1b1-4494-b299-32dd4a7f8dfe]]
years.p: Over Easter weekend at Southern Records' Wood Green studio, [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]] cut four songs. Dischord says it was the last time the two recorded together.

[[Guy Picciotto|f8200cea-b5e9-4145-b5a5-1d0838f2c288]], [[Eddie Janney|323dd1dd-23e4-45ce-9aa9-c5492096d604]] and [[Brendan Canty|8b505ef0-c5a7-4deb-bc32-27c882f3c40e]], all of [[Rites of Spring|b2ff1a6d-9198-4646-b068-8965242d245b]], start One Last Wish with Michael Hampton on guitar.

years.h: Egg Hunt tries to become a full band
years.p: MacKaye and Nelson look for a line-up among ex-members of [[Gray Matter|c9065214-ba09-4c2c-b341-35713b702264]]. In Dischord's words, it wasn't meant to be.

years.h: "Emocore" sticks to Embrace, and MacKaye hates it
years.p: Ian MacKaye, in 1986 interview footage, on the label fans had hung on Embrace and Rites of Spring. Dag Nasty's Brian Baker told Parade in 2025 he made the word up at a December 1985 show to mock Rites of Spring.
years.xp:
Embrace, Dag Nasty and Rites of Spring shared a bill on December 4, 1985. Baker had played with MacKaye in Minor Threat.

For MacKaye the point was to strip away hardcore's posturing, not to start a subgenre. The label outlived both bands by decades.

years.h: "Dance of Days" live at the 9:30 Club, 1986
yt: "Dance of Days" live at the 9:30 Club, 1986

eras.title: The album arrives late
eras.text: Embrace's only album came out more than a year after the last show, from a band that no longer existed. By then MacKaye had Fugazi, which took Embrace's slower, searching sound and made something much bigger.

years.h: The album lands a year after the split
years.p: Recorded at Inner Ear from November 1985 to February 1986, Embrace came out as Dischord No. 24 in September 1987. Mark Jenkins, co-author of Dance of Days, heard sermons against greed, delusion and self-destruction.
years.xp:
[[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]] engineered in Arlington. [[Eddie Janney|323dd1dd-23e4-45ce-9aa9-c5492096d604]] of Rites of Spring plays guitar on one track and shares the production credit with the band and MacKaye. Fourteen songs, 33 minutes.

Trouser Press called the instrumentals strong and muscular, an effective backdrop for MacKaye. Money and Last Song point straight at Fugazi.

years.h: Fugazi play their first show at the Wilson Center
years.p: [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] debut on September 3 with Brendan Canty on drums. Guy Picciotto is singing with them within weeks: two Rites of Spring players Embrace had shared 1985 bills with.

years.h: Hampton and Hanson team up again in Manifesto
years.p: Embrace's guitarist and drummer, bandmates since SOA, start Manifesto.

eras.title: Other bands cover the record
eras.text: Embrace never reunited, but the record kept getting reissued and covered. A younger generation of hardcore and pop-punk bands paid it back in the most D.C. way available: a benefit.

years.h: CD and cassette, with new cover art
years.p: Embrace's album is reissued on CD and cassette with alternate cover art.

years.h: Bands cover Embrace for homeless shelters
years.p: Trustkill Records releases Land of Greed... World of Need, with [[Avail|d67ff511-57b8-4d02-94d3-6c6a331c2ae4]], [[Rancid|24f8d8a5-269b-475c-a1cb-792990b0b2ee]] and [[Lifetime|c9329809-8510-45b9-9202-5640398ddaee]] among the bands covering Embrace. Proceeds go to homeless shelters.

yt: Dance of Days, live at the 9:30 Club, 1986
years.h: Chad Clark remasters it, adding two alternate takes
years.p: Chad Clark remasters Embrace at Silver Sonya, and alternate versions of Money and Dance of Days are added.

years.h: Ivor Hanson writes a memoir about washing windows
years.p: Ivor Hanson publishes Life on the Ledge: Reflections of a New York City Window Cleaner, about his years on the ledges of Manhattan buildings. Two Dollar Radio puts it out.

years.h: Red vinyl, then a new master for the LP
years.p: After a red vinyl pressing in 2008, Jason Ward remasters Embrace's LP at Chicago Mastering Service.
